metadata.title: TIMSS 2011: Mathematische und naturwissenschaftliche Kompetenzen von Grundschulkindern in Deutschland im internationalen Vergleich

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: TIMSS 2011 uses a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design (schools, then intact classes) and computes a statistical weight for each tested student to correct for unequal selection probabilities and nonresponse. In this German report, the analytic results are based on the international scaling and reporting framework, which applies these sampling weights when estimating means and percentages. Because the design is clustered (not simple random sampling), standard errors are not computed with conventional formulas; instead, Jackknife Repeated Replication (JRR) is used to estimate sampling and measurement uncertainty. The manuscript does not name a specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that TIMSS computes and uses student weights and JRR replicate procedures for inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report describes that TIMSS uses plausible values (five draws) for achievement scaling, but it does not document a specific missing-data strategy for questionnaire or background variables (e.g., listwise deletion vs. multiple imputation) in the provided text. This is a reporting gap because TIMSS background questionnaires can contain missing responses, and the choice of missing-data handling can affect estimated relationships between context variables and achievement. The manuscript focuses on the official scaling and sampling/replication framework rather than detailing the downstream missing-data procedure for covariates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The German TIMSS 2011 sample was drawn as a stratified cluster design with 200 initially selected schools, reduced to 198 schools after excluding two (an international school with English instruction and a private school not required to participate). Of the 4,229 students in 197 tested schools, 3,995 students actually participated in the TIMSS test; non-participation (n=234) was due to exclusion reasons, leaving school before the test day, or absence on the test day. The report also states that the international target population exclusions are limited (max 5% internationally) and that interpretation of means requires at least 85% of students to have scorable performance values, with a minimum number of test items successfully completed.

data.outcome_summary: This volume reports TIMSS 2011 results for Germany’s Grade 4 students in mathematics (and also describes the broader TIMSS design). The study uses TIMSS’s international scaling framework based on IRT and plausible values: student achievement on the TIMSS scale is estimated using five plausible values drawn from conditional distributions, and inference uses sampling weights with Jackknife Repeated Replication (JRR). For mathematics, Germany’s mean is 528 points, significantly above the international mean (491) and above EU (519) and OECD (521) averages, with no significant change versus TIMSS 2007 (528 vs 525). The distribution shows 3% at Level I and only 5% at Level V, and the report highlights domain-specific patterns: improvements since 2007 are significant in Geometry/Measures (+9) and Data Display (+14), while Arithmetics does not significantly change. Limitations include that the excerpted text does not specify missing-data handling for background variables and that the analysis is descriptive/benchmark-based rather than ML predictive modeling.
